GaugeQuant: Online Learning of Quantization-Optimal Bases from LLM Symmetries

Miguel P. Bento Affiliation: Independent Researcher Affiliation: Lisbon, Portugal Email: miguel.pedra.bento@tecnico.ulisboa.pt    João Seabra Affiliation: Independent Researcher Affiliation: Lisbon, Portugal Email: joao.seabra@tecnico.ulisboa.pt
Abstract

Transformers are known to have internal continuous symmetries that leave outputs invariant, while modifying quantization. GaugeQuant leverages this in-training by introducing a LogSumExp term to the loss that breaks the symmetries, thus selecting a basis that minimizes activation outliers. A stop-gradient operator ensures that only rotation matrices are updated, yielding the language modeling objective completely unaltered. Our requires no specific calibration data, no quantization simulation, and adds negligible training overhead. With the LLaMA-2 7B model under W4A4 quantization with group size 128, perplexity drops from 8.22 to 6.73, competing with post-training methods that require frozen models and calibration datasets. Under W4A16, perplexity drops from 11.16 to 5.45. Code is available at https://github.com/MPedraBento/gauge-quant.

1 Introduction

The capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) are only attained nowadays with massive computational and memory resources. In fact, the transformer Vaswani et al. (2017) architectures at the core of state of the art LLMs contain billions of parameters, requiring multiple GPUs for both training and inference Zhao et al. (2026).

To reduce the memory footprint of LLMs, several quantization techniques have been put forward where different variables (e.g. weights and activations) of the model are compressed into lower-precision formats. Post-training quantization (PTQ) methods are the most commonly seen in the literature, where model variables are quantized after the LLM is fully trained. The scale factors needed to pack the data into fewer bits are computed using small calibration datasets, making this kind of quantization procedures computationally inexpensive. However, PTQ also leads to degradation in the LLM performance, caused by the presence of outliers in the quantized variables distribution. Especially usual among activations Dettmers et al. (2022); Xiao et al. (2023), outliers stretch the quantization range, leaving fewer bits available for representing the most frequent values.

In this paper, we propose GaugeQuant: an in-training quantization mechanism that mitigates PTQ’s drawbacks by learning a preferred basis across different boundaries of the LLM architecture during training.11 1 We use “gauge” in the sense of a redundant internal parametrization that leaves observables invariant, analogous to gauge freedom in field theory, though here the symmetry is global (position-independent) at each boundary rather than local in the differential-geometric sense. The main source of inspiration for our approach is SpinQuant Liu et al. (2024), where outliers are suppressed by learning the best orthogonal rotations of the network variables for that effect. Those rotations can be performed because of LLMs’ symmetries, which make their outputs invariant under such transformations. While retaining this idea, we introduce a different loss function that removes outliers during training and the need for static calibration datasets. Besides the usual cross-entropy loss, which minimizes the difference between the model’s predicted probability distribution and the true probability distribution of the next token, we include a second term that penalizes outliers among the rotated boundary activations. More specifically, the latter takes the form of a LogSumExp function: a smooth, dense approximation of the infinite norm Nesterov (2005) that routes gradient to every dimension, and not just the single maximum outlier.

This paper is structured as follows: In the following section, we introduce in more detail ideas from previous works that helped us shape our approach to in-training quantization. In Section 3, we do an overview of the LLM symmetries. The most important aspects of the LLM training procedure using GaugeQuant are presented in Section 4. Our results, obtained after applying GaugeQuant to Qwen-2.5 0.5B Qwen et al. (2025) and LLaMA-2 7B Touvron et al. (2023) are shown in Section 5, using the WikiText-2 Merity et al. (2016) dataset as benchmark. A discussion of our results and broader implications of them is made in Section 6. In Section 7, we describe the limitations of our approach. Finally, in Section 8, we draw some concluding remarks about our work.

2 Background and related Work

LLM PTQ. In the context of LLMs, quantization is mostly motivated by the prohibitive cost of deploying those models for inference. Earlier approaches like ZeroQuant Yao et al. (2022), LLM.int8() Dettmers et al. (2022) and nuQmm Park et al. (2022) tackled very large models at reasonable runtimes by rounding just the weights to the nearest quantization level. GPTQ Frantar et al. (2022), which is commonly used as a PTQ baseline in more recent works, brought a considerable improvement over those methods, allowing the usage of a single GPU for performing inference with Generative Pre-trained Transformer (GPT) models with 175 billion parameters.

Unlike GPTQ where only the model weights are quantized, more recent PTQ schemes provide mechanisms to quantize activations as well. SmoothQuant Xiao et al. (2023) and AWQ Lin et al. (2024) are some of the earliest examples of those schemes, in which the quantization difficulty is migrated between activations and weights.

Exploiting LLM symmetries: Neural network symmetries are a research topic of their own that may give valuable insights about parameter redundancies within models (see for example Hashimoto et al. (2024)). Those redundancies have been exploited by several authors to reduce the complexity of LLMs. For example, SliceGPT Ashkboos et al. (2024a) introduces a post-training sparsification scheme, which takes advantage of the LLM computational invariance – the designation given by the authors to the output’s invariance under any orthogonal transformation of the weight matrices. In the context of quantization, symmetries are usually exploited for reducing outliers. Taking inspiration from the computational invariance described in SliceGPT, Quarot Ashkboos et al. (2024b) applies randomized Hadamard rotations at internal boundaries of the model, in order to eliminate activation outliers. RoLoRA Huang et al. (2024) couples this idea with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) Hu et al. (2021) to enhance the fine-tuning efficiency of the model. SpinQuant Liu et al. (2024) takes a step forward in outlier suppression by letting the model learn the rotations that optimize the performance of the (quantized) LLM. To this end, SpinQuant employs the Cayley Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD), which is especially proficient at optimizing orthonormal matrices Li et al. (2020). Building upon Quarot and SpinQuant, ReSpinQuant Kim et al. (2026) assigns a unique rotation matrix for each layer. The advent of reasoning LLMs also motivated the proposal of ParoQuant Liang et al. (2026): a PTQ scheme tailored to these models, which combines channel-wise scaling with rotations.

While all the works mentioned thus far apply quantization post-training, some authors have put forward quantization-aware training (QAT) techniques that still apply the idea of rotating model parameters to remove outliers. One example is RoSTE Wei et al. (2025), which combines these rotations with quantization-aware supervised fine-tuning. Another example is HALO Ashkboos et al. (2025), where Hadamard rotations are placed in both the forward and backward passes. Finally, it is also worth mentioning Park et al. (2025), which proposes an outlier-safe in-training framework that, like GaugeQuant, targets quantization robustness during training, though via architectural modifications (optimizer and normalization changes) rather than learned rotations.

3 Symmetries of LLMs

Multi-head attention (MHA) can be described for a single head hh. Given input X∈ℝN×dmodelX\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d_{\text{model}}}, the network computes

Q(h)=X​WQ(h),K(h)=X​WK(h),V(h)=X​WV(h),Q^{(h)}=XW_{Q}^{(h)},\quad K^{(h)}=XW_{K}^{(h)},\quad V^{(h)}=XW_{V}^{(h)}\,, (1)

where WQ(h),WK(h),WV(h)∈ℝdmodel×dkW_{Q}^{(h)},W_{K}^{(h)},W_{V}^{(h)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}\times d_{k}} and dkd_{k} is the head dimension. With Rotary Positional Embeddings (RoPE) Su et al. (2024), the pre-softmax scores are

Sm,n(h)=(Xm​WQ(h)​Θm)​(Xn​WK(h)​Θn)⊤dk,S_{m,n}^{(h)}=\frac{(X_{m}W_{Q}^{(h)}\Theta_{m})(X_{n}W_{K}^{(h)}\Theta_{n})^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_{k}}}\,, (2)

where Θm\Theta_{m} is the RoPE matrix (block-diagonal 2D rotations) at position mm. The head output is

Y(h)=softmax​(S(h))​V(h)​WO(h),Y^{(h)}=\text{softmax}(S^{(h)})\,V^{(h)}\,W_{O}^{(h)}\,, (3)

with WO(h)∈ℝdk×dmodelW_{O}^{(h)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{k}\times d_{\text{model}}}. The SwiGLU MLP block Shazeer (2020) computes

MLP​(X)=[σ⁡(X​Wgate)⊙(X​Wup)]⏟H​Wdown,\text{MLP}(X)=\underbrace{\left[\sigma(XW_{\text{gate}})\odot(XW_{\text{up}})\right]}_{H}W_{\text{down}}\,, (4)

where σ\sigma is SiLU and ⊙\odot the Hadamard product.

3.1 Invariances of the transformer

These linear maps possess continuous symmetries, transformations that leave the network output exactly unchanged.

V–O boundary.

Let RV∈S​O​(dk)R_{V}\in SO(d_{k}). Attention computes a weighted sum of value vectors, so the rotation passes through linearly

softmax​(S(h))​(V(h)​RV)​(RV⊤​WO(h))=Y(h).\text{softmax}(S^{(h)})(V^{(h)}R_{V})(R_{V}^{\top}W_{O}^{(h)})=Y^{(h)}\,. (5)

This reveals a continuous S​O​(dk)SO(d_{k}) symmetry per KV head. For Grouped Query Attention (GQA), where nheads/nkvn_{\text{heads}}/n_{\text{kv}} query heads share each KV head, all heads in a group share the same rotation, yielding S​O​(dk)nkvSO(d_{k})^{n_{\text{kv}}} total degrees of freedom.

Q–K boundary.

A rotation RQR_{Q} must commute with RoPE: RQ​Θm=Θm​RQR_{Q}\Theta_{m}=\Theta_{m}R_{Q}. Since Θm\Theta_{m} is composed of 2D rotations, RQR_{Q} is restricted to a block-diagonal matrix of independent planar rotations, reducing the symmetry from S​O​(dk)SO(d_{k}) to the torus U​(1)dk/2U(1)^{d_{k}/2}, too few parameters to meaningfully suppress outliers. We do not exploit this smaller symmetry.

MLP boundary.

The linear map H​WdownHW_{\text{down}} admits the same invariance

H​Wdown=(H​R)​(R⊤​Wdown),R∈S​O​(dff).HW_{\text{down}}=(HR)(R^{\top}W_{\text{down}})\,,\quad R\in SO(d_{\text{ff}})\,. (6)

However, unlike the attention case, RR cannot be fully absorbed into weights. Absorbing RR upstream would require σ⁡(X​Wgate​R)⊙(X​Wup​R)=[σ⁡(X​Wgate)⊙(X​Wup)]​R\sigma(XW_{\text{gate}}R)\odot(XW_{\text{up}}R)=[\sigma(XW_{\text{gate}})\odot(XW_{\text{up}})]R, which fails because: (i) SiLU is element-wise but RR mixes dimensions, so σ⁡(v​R)≠σ⁡(v)​R\sigma(vR)\neq\sigma(v)R; and (ii) the Hadamard product satisfies (a​R)⊙(b​R)≠(a⊙b)​R(aR)\odot(bR)\neq(a\odot b)R for non-trivial rotations. Therefore R⊤R^{\top} can be permanently fused into WdownW_{\text{down}}, but the multiplication H⋅RH\cdot R must remain as a runtime operation, analogously to Liu et al. (2024); Ashkboos et al. (2024b).

3.2 Basis choice for quantization

These symmetries mean the parameter space contains degrees of freedom with no effect on exact outputs, they represent a choice of coordinate basis. Let Θ\Theta denote standard parameters and ΘR\Theta_{R} the transformed parameters. At full precision

y^​(x,ΘR)=y^​(x,Θ).\hat{y}(x;\Theta_{R})=\hat{y}(x;\Theta)\,. (7)

However, uniform quantization Q⁡(⋅)Q(\cdot) is element-wise and non-linear, so it does not commute with rotations

y^​(x,Q⁡(ΘR))≠y^​(x,Q⁡(Θ)).\hat{y}(x;Q(\Theta_{R}))\neq\hat{y}(x;Q(\Theta))\,. (8)

The quantization grid step Δ∝‖v‖∞\Delta\propto\|v\|_{\infty} is dictated by the worst outlier (see Appendix A). The optimal basis is therefore the one that distributes activation mass uniformly across dimensions. The central question is how to find this basis efficiently during training.

4 In-training gauge optimization

Post-training methods such as SpinQuant Liu et al. (2024) optimize RR by minimizing the quantization error on a frozen model with a static calibration set

ℒPTQ​(R)=‖X​W−Q⁡(X​W​R)​R⊤‖F2.\mathcal{L}_{\text{PTQ}}(R)=\|XW-Q(XWR)R^{\top}\|_{F}^{2}\,. (9)

This requires the non-differentiable Q⁡(⋅)Q(\cdot) operator and a frozen model, thus fundamentally incompatible with in-training optimization.

A differentiable proxy for quantization

We replace the explicit quantization simulation with a smooth proxy. Since Δ∝‖v‖∞\Delta\propto\|v\|_{\infty}, suppressing the L∞L_{\infty} norm of the rotated activations directly reduces quantization error. We use the LogSumExp as a dense, differentiable approximation

ℒrot​(R)=1β​log⁡(∑iexp⁡(β​|zi|)),z=sg​(H)⋅R,\mathcal{L}_{\text{rot}}(R)=\frac{1}{\beta}\log\left(\sum_{i}\exp\left(\beta\,|z_{i}|\right)\right)\,,\quad z=\text{sg}(H)\cdot R\,, (10)

where HH denotes the boundary activations (H=X​WV(h)H=XW_{V}^{(h)} for attention, H=σ⁡(X​Wgate)⊙(X​Wup)H=\sigma(XW_{\text{gate}})\odot(XW_{\text{up}}) for MLP) and sg​(⋅)\text{sg}(\cdot) is the stop-gradient operator and β>0\beta>0 controls the approximation. The gradient

∂ℒrot∂|zi|=exp⁡(β​|zi|)∑jexp⁡(β​|zj|),\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}_{\text{rot}}}{\partial|z_{i}|}=\frac{\exp(\beta\,|z_{i}|)}{\sum_{j}\exp(\beta\,|z_{j}|)}\,, (11)

smoothly addresses outliers while yielding non-zero values for smaller numbers.22 2 We note that the gradient is exactly the softmax function with inverse temperature β\beta. Eq. (10) is not rotationally invariant, and thus, adding it to the loss explicitly breaks the symmetry, selecting a unique, quantization-optimal basis.

The stop-gradient operator ensures a clean separation between the language modeling and gauge objectives

ℒtotal=ℒCE​(X,Θ)+λ​ℒrot​(sg​(H)⋅R),\mathcal{L}_{\text{total}}=\mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}}(X;\Theta)+\lambda\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{rot}}(\text{sg}(H)\cdot R)\,, (12)

which guarantees

∇Wℒtotal=∇WℒCE,∇Rℒtotal=λ​∇Rℒrot.\nabla_{W}\mathcal{L}_{\text{total}}=\nabla_{W}\mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}},\quad\nabla_{R}\mathcal{L}_{\text{total}}=\lambda\,\nabla_{R}\mathcal{L}_{\text{rot}}\,. (13)

The weights adapt to the evolving rotation through the CE loss alone, while the rotation parameters are updated exclusively by LogSumExp. The two objectives are orthogonal by construction.

A symmetry of the training

Up to this point, we have discussed the symmetries as special orthogonal matrices and purposely ignored the role of weight decay. So, why must the gauge be a special orthogonal matrix rather than an arbitrary invertible matrix? The answer lies in weight decay. Standard training regularizes with ‖W‖F2\|W\|_{F}^{2}, which is invariant under orthogonal transformations, but not under general linear maps. Therefore, O⁡(d)O(d) is a unique continuous symmetry group that is simultaneously an invariance of the forward pass, norm-preserving for activations and an invariant of weight decay (see Appendix B).

While full orthogonal matrices could be used, naive gradient descent on RR leaves the orthogonal manifold after a single step. Instead, we learn a skew-symmetric matrix A=−A⊤A=-A^{\top} and map it to S​O​(d)SO(d) via the Cayley transform

R=(I−A)​(I+A)−1.R=(I-A)(I+A)^{-1}\,. (14)

Thus, without loss of generality we choose S​O​(d)⊂O⁡(d)SO(d)\subset O(d), which admits a smooth Cayley parametrization.

Block-diagonal structure for the MLP.

A full S​O​(dff)SO(d_{\text{ff}}) rotation requires O⁡(dff3)O(d_{\text{ff}}^{3}) matrix inversion, prohibitive for dff=11,008d_{\text{ff}}=11{,}008. We parametrize the MLP gauge as a block-diagonal rotation

RMLP=⨁k=1dff/bRk,Rk∈S​O​(b),R_{\text{MLP}}=\bigoplus_{k=1}^{d_{\text{ff}}/b}R_{k}\,,\quad R_{k}\in SO(b)\,, (15)

with block size b=64b=64. Each block is independently mapped via its own Cayley transform with cost O⁡(b3)O(b^{3}), giving total cost O⁡(dff⋅b2)O(d_{\text{ff}}\cdot b^{2}), linear in the hidden dimension. The block structure is itself orthogonal, preserving the gauge invariance. All matrix inversions and weight fusions are computed in float32 to prevent orthogonality drift from reduced-precision arithmetic.

5 Empirical studies

We evaluate GaugeQuant on two models: Qwen-2.5 0.5B Qwen et al. (2025) and LLaMA-2 7B Touvron et al. (2023). Training streams text from C4 Raffel et al. (2019) for 8192 steps with batch size 1, sequence length 512, and λ=0.1\lambda=0.1. This corresponds to a short continued-training run (∼4{\sim}4M tokens); integration into full-scale pretraining is left for future work. The rotation loss learning rate is 2×10−42\times 10^{-4}, while base weights use 2×10−52\times 10^{-5} (full fine-tuning for Qwen, LoRA r=16r{=}16 for LLaMA-2). Evaluation measures perplexity on WikiText-2 Merity et al. (2016) (2048 tokens).

Quantization setup.

We simulate symmetric min-max quantization on all seven linear layers (q/k/v/o_proj, gate/up/down_proj). Weights are quantized per output channel, activations per token. We report three regimes: W4A16 (4-bit weights, full-precision activations), W4A4 g128 (4-bit activations with group size 128) and W4A4 per-token (4-bit activations with a single scale per token, the strictest setting).

Baselines.

For each regime we report three conditions: (1) Baseline: the pretrained HuggingFace model quantized directly; (2) Control: fine-tuned with the same training budget but without the gauge loss; (3) GaugeQuant: fine-tuned jointly with gauge optimization.

5.1 Results

W4A16.

On LLaMA-2 7B, GaugeQuant achieves 5.45 PPL under 4-bit weight quantization, a 51% reduction in quantization-induced degradation compared to the baseline (11.16), approaching the ∼6.2{\sim}6.2 reported by SpinQuant under comparable evaluation conditions. On Qwen-2.5 0.5B, the reduction is 35% (25.62 →\to 16.76). Although ℒrot\mathcal{L}_{\text{rot}} targets activation outliers directly, the fused rotation also transforms the weight matrices (WVnew=R⊤​WVW_{V}^{\text{new}}=R^{\top}W_{V}, Wdownnew=Wdown​RW_{\text{down}}^{\text{new}}=W_{\text{down}}R), redistributing weight values and reducing weight quantization error as a secondary effect.

W4A4 g128.

Under group-128 activation quantization (the regime used by SpinQuant), GaugeQuant reduces perplexity from 8.22 to 6.73 on LLaMA-2 7B (18% reduction) and from 187.8 to 61.2 on Qwen-2.5 0.5B (67% reduction). Fine-tuning alone (Control) provides no benefit and can worsen quantization performance, confirming that the improvement is attributable to the gauge rotation.

W4A4 per-token.

Per-token activation quantization (one scale across the full hidden dimension) remains a regime where all methods fail: both models collapse to unusable perplexity regardless of rotation. The relative improvements confirm that the gauge suppresses activation outliers, but viable W4A4 inference requires group quantization as shown above.

6 Discussion and Broader Implications

We show that the continuous symmetries of transformer architectures can be used online during training, rather than only post-hoc on frozen models. The method is complementary to post-training approaches, as one could integrate GaugeQuant into any training run (including pretraining at scale) to obtain a quantization-friendly model, then optionally refine with SpinQuant for further gains. Specifically, the gauge framework generalizes beyond quantization. Any hardware constraint that breaks rotational symmetry (structured sparsity patterns, mixed-precision formats, low-rank decompositions) could in principle be targeted by a similar non-invariant proxy loss.

7 Limitations

Analogously to SpinQuant, our method relies on an online MLP rotation that adds a small cost to inference. This arises because the SwiGLU non-linearity prevents absorbing RR upstream, requiring a block-diagonal rotation (b=64b=64) at runtime. This block structure is itself a design choice that limits outlier redistribution across block boundaries. This structure by itself is choice that can limit the possibility of further enhancing results.

Another limitation is that The LogSumExp proxy suppresses all large activations indiscriminately, which may reduce the model’s capability to encode distinctions between similar outputs. An additional proxy targeting weight outliers could mitigate this effect.

Finally, experiments are limited to two models (0.5B and 7B), with larger models possibly exhibiting different outlier dynamics.

8 Conclusion

We introduced GaugeQuant, a method that exploits the continuous symmetries of transformer architectures to learn quantization-optimal bases during training. By adding a differentiable LogSumExp loss term that explicitly breaks the gauge symmetry, the method selects a basis that suppress activation outliers without interfering with the language modeling objective. On LLaMA-2 7B, GaugeQuant reduces W4A4 g128 degradation by 18% ,and W4A16 quantization degradation by 51%, with no calibration data and negligible training overhead. Future work includes combining GaugeQuant with post-training rotation methods, exploring joint activation-weight incoherence proxies that more closely approximate the true quantization error, and scaling to larger models.

Appendix A Quantization error and the L∞L_{\infty} norm

We briefly justify why minimizing ‖v‖∞\|v\|_{\infty} reduces quantization error. Consider symmetric uniform quantization of a vector v∈ℝdv\in\mathbb{R}^{d} to bb bits. The quantized representation is

v^i=Δ⋅clamp​(⌊viΔ⌉,−2b−1, 2b−1−1),Δ=‖v‖∞2b−1−1.\hat{v}_{i}=\Delta\cdot\text{clamp}\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac{v_{i}}{\Delta}\right\rceil,\,-2^{b-1},\,2^{b-1}-1\right),\quad\Delta=\frac{\|v\|_{\infty}}{2^{b-1}-1}\,. (16)

The per-element quantization error is bounded by |vi−v^i|≤Δ/2|v_{i}-\hat{v}_{i}|\leq\Delta/2. The total squared error satisfies

‖v−v^‖22≤d⋅Δ24=d4​(2b−1−1)2​‖v‖∞2.\|v-\hat{v}\|_{2}^{2}\leq d\cdot\frac{\Delta^{2}}{4}=\frac{d}{4(2^{b-1}-1)^{2}}\|v\|_{\infty}^{2}\,. (17)

Therefore, for fixed dd and bb, the worst-case quantization error is directly proportional to ‖v‖∞2\|v\|_{\infty}^{2}. An orthogonal rotation RR preserves ‖v‖2\|v\|_{2} but can reduce ‖v​R‖∞\|vR\|_{\infty} (redistributing mass from outlier dimensions). The optimal rotation satisfies ‖v​R∗‖∞=‖v‖2/d\|vR^{*}\|_{\infty}=\|v\|_{2}/\sqrt{d} (the isotropic limit), achievable when all coordinates have equal magnitude.

Note that this bound is tight only when vv has no clipped entries. In practice, for highly non-uniform vv, the actual quantization error depends on the full distribution of viv_{i}, not just ‖v‖∞\|v\|_{\infty}. Furthermore, this analysis addresses activation quantization; weight quantization error depends on ‖W​R‖∞\|WR\|_{\infty} along the channel dimension, which our current proxy does not directly penalize (see Section 7).

Appendix B Weight decay breaks G​L​(d)GL(d) into O⁡(d)O(d) as the maximal symmetry

We prove that O⁡(d)O(d) is the largest continuous matrix group whose action on weights is a symmetry of the standard weight decay regularizer.

Proposition 1.

Let G⊆G​L​(d)G\subseteq GL(d) be a connected Lie subgroup such that ‖W​M‖F=‖W‖F\|WM\|_{F}=\|W\|_{F} for all W∈ℝm×dW\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d} and all M∈GM\in G. Then G⊆O⁡(d)G\subseteq O(d).

Proof.

The Frobenius norm satisfies ‖W​M‖F2=tr⁡(M⊤​W⊤​W​M)\|WM\|_{F}^{2}=\tr(M^{\top}W^{\top}WM). For this to equal ‖W‖F2=tr⁡(W⊤​W)\|W\|_{F}^{2}=\tr(W^{\top}W) for all WW, we require

tr⁡(M⊤​S​M)=tr⁡(S)∀S⪰0,\tr(M^{\top}SM)=\tr(S)\quad\forall\,S\succeq 0\,, (18)

where S=W⊤​WS=W^{\top}W ranges over all positive semidefinite matrices as WW varies. By the cyclic property of the trace, this is equivalent to tr⁡(S⋅M​M⊤)=tr⁡(S)\tr(S\cdot MM^{\top})=\tr(S), or

tr⁡(S⁡(M​M⊤−I))=0∀S⪰0.\tr\bigl(S(MM^{\top}-I)\bigr)=0\quad\forall\,S\succeq 0\,. (19)

Suppose M​M⊤−I≠0MM^{\top}-I\neq 0. Then M​M⊤−IMM^{\top}-I is a nonzero symmetric matrix and therefore has at least one nonzero eigenvalue λ≠0\lambda\neq 0 with corresponding eigenvector vv. Choosing S=v​v⊤⪰0S=vv^{\top}\succeq 0, we obtain tr⁡(v​v⊤​(M​M⊤−I))=v⊤​(M​M⊤−I)​v=λ≠0\tr(vv^{\top}(MM^{\top}-I))=v^{\top}(MM^{\top}-I)v=\lambda\neq 0, which is a contradiction. Therefore M​M⊤=IMM^{\top}=I, hence M∈O⁡(d)M\in O(d). ∎

Since the Cayley transform parametrizes S​O​(d)SO(d), our restriction to this subgroup is without loss of generality. The LogSumExp penalty depends on |zi||z_{i}|, which is invariant under sign flips, so every minimum within O⁡(d)O(d) is attainable within S​O​(d)SO(d).
